plan: Third ACT English passage: an original profile (~300 words, invented town and person). NO CHANGE is the key for only 2 of 11 items, keys are spread, and choices are balanced in length. Includes one essay-level goal item, with the tool updated to allow underline: null when essay_level is true.

passages.title: The Last Sign Painter in Calder
passages.genre: profile (original; Calder and Marrow are invented)
passages.text:
In the river town of Calder, nearly every storefront sign was painted by hand, and most of them {{1|was}} painted by the same woman. For forty years, Edith Marrow climbed ladders with a {{2|brush a can of enamel, and a steady hand}}, lettering the names of bakeries, barbershops, and hardware stores {{3|onto there}} windows and walls.

Marrow learned the trade from her father, who {{4|had painted signs}} for the town since before she was born. {{5|He taught her to mix colors, to space letters by eye, and that a sign should be read from across the street.}} She practiced on scrap boards in the garage, painting the alphabet hundreds of times until her strokes were {{6|identical; even}} her father could not tell them from his own.

When vinyl lettering machines arrived in the 1990s, many of Marrow's customers switched. The machines were faster and {{7|cheaper, however,}} the stickers they produced {{8|got kind of messed up}} within a few years. One by one, the shop owners came back. "A machine can make a letter," one barber told a reporter, "but it can't make a sign."

Today Marrow is in her seventies and no longer climbs ladders. {{9|Still, she enjoys gardening and reading in her spare time.}} {{10|Her students, many of whom are young and in their twenties,}} say they come for the craft but stay for the patience it teaches.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: most of them was painted by the same woman
candidates.explanation: "Most of them" refers to the signs, which are plural, so the verb must be plural: "were painted." The past tense matches the forty years described.

A.rationale: "Was" is singular, but "most of them" refers to many signs.

B.rationale: "Has been" is singular and shifts the tense.

hints: What does "them" refer to?
Is "most of them" singular or plural here?

strategy.explanation: Most of + plural noun takes a plural verb.

candidates.remember: "Most of" takes its number from the noun after "of."

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.B: brush; a can of enamel; and a steady hand
choices.C: brush, a can of enamel and, a steady hand
choices.D: brush, a can of enamel, and a steady hand

candidates.evidence: climbed ladders with a brush a can of enamel, and a steady hand
candidates.explanation: The three items in the series need commas between them: "a brush, a can of enamel, and a steady hand."

B.rationale: Semicolons separate items in a series only when the items already contain commas.

C.rationale: The comma belongs before "and," not after it.

hints: How many items are in the list?
Where should the commas go?

strategy.explanation: Series of three: item, item, and item.

candidates.remember: Separate simple series items with commas.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.explanation: The windows and walls belong to the businesses, so the possessive "their" is needed.

C.rationale: This keeps the wrong word and splits "onto" unnecessarily.

hints: Whose windows and walls are they?
Which spelling shows ownership?

strategy.explanation: Test "they are" and "in that place"; neither fits, so use the possessive.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: who had painted signs for the town since before she was born
candidates.explanation: Her father's painting began before she was born and continued up to the past time being described, so the past perfect "had painted" is correct.

B.rationale: Present tense clashes with the past-tense narrative.

C.rationale: Present perfect connects to the present, but this describes the past.

D.rationale: "Painting" leaves the clause without a complete verb.

hints: When did the father paint signs relative to the story's time?
Which tense describes an action before another past time?

strategy.explanation: Only one choice keeps a complete past-time verb.

candidates.remember: Past perfect: an action before another past moment.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.B: He taught her mixing colors, to space letters by eye, and that signs should be readable from across the street.
choices.C: He taught her to mix colors, to space letters by eye, and to make every sign readable from across the street.
choices.D: He taught her to mix colors, spacing letters by eye, and making every sign readable from across the street.

candidates.evidence: He taught her to mix colors, to space letters by eye, and that a sign should be read from across the street.
candidates.explanation: Items in a list should share the same form. C uses three parallel infinitives: "to mix," "to space," "to make."

A.rationale: The third item switches from an infinitive to a "that" clause.

B.rationale: This mixes a gerund, an infinitive and a clause.

D.rationale: This mixes an infinitive with two gerunds.

hints: What form do the first two items take?
Make the third match.

strategy.explanation: Choose the version whose three items all start with "to."

candidates.remember: Keep list items in the same grammatical form.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: until her strokes were identical; even her father could not tell them from his own
candidates.explanation: "Her strokes were identical" and "even her father could not tell them from his own" are both complete clauses. A semicolon correctly joins them.

B.rationale: A comma alone between two complete clauses is a comma splice.

C.rationale: With no punctuation the clauses run together.

D.rationale: "Which even her father could not tell …" is ungrammatical.

hints: Is each side of the punctuation a complete sentence?
What can join two complete sentences without a conjunction?

strategy.explanation: Two independent clauses, no conjunction: semicolon.

candidates.remember: Semicolon: two complete sentences, no conjunction.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: The machines were faster and cheaper, however, the stickers they produced
candidates.explanation: "However" begins a new independent clause here, so it must follow a semicolon (or period) and be followed by a comma: "cheaper; however, the stickers …"

A.rationale: Commas on both sides of "however" create a comma splice between two independent clauses.

D.rationale: A single comma before "however" still splices the clauses.

hints: Are there complete sentences on both sides of "however"?
"However" is not a conjunction like "but."

strategy.explanation: Conjunctive adverb between clauses: semicolon before, comma after.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: the stickers they produced got kind of messed up within a few years
candidates.explanation: "Peeled and faded" names exactly what went wrong and fits the essay's tone. The other choices are vague or too casual.

A.rationale: "Got kind of messed up" is vague and too informal.

B.rationale: "Experienced problems" is vague; it does not say what happened.

D.rationale: "Were not so good" is vague and informal.

hints: Which choice tells the reader exactly what happened to the stickers?
Which matches the essay's tone?

strategy.explanation: Predict a specific verb, then choose the most precise option.

candidates.remember: Prefer precise words over vague ones.

candidates.subskill: Concluding sentence that links to earlier content
candidates.stem: Which choice most effectively connects the final paragraph to the essay's description of how Marrow learned her craft?

choices.B: Still, vinyl machines remain popular in larger cities.
choices.C: Still, many of her father's signs have been painted over.
choices.D: Still, she teaches a weekend class in the old garage, where a new generation practices the alphabet on scrap boards.

candidates.evidence: She practiced on scrap boards in the garage, painting the alphabet hundreds of times
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 2 describes Marrow practicing the alphabet on scrap boards in the garage. D echoes that detail and shows the craft being passed on, which also sets up the next sentence about her students.

A.rationale: Gardening and reading do not connect to how she learned the craft, and they don't introduce the students mentioned next.

B.rationale: Vinyl machines relate to paragraph 3, not to how she learned.

C.rationale: Her father's signs are mentioned, but this does not connect to her training or her students.

hints: What did Marrow do in the garage when she was learning?
The next sentence mentions "Her students"; which choice introduces them?

strategy.explanation: Find the matching details in paragraph 2.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.B: Her students, many of whom are in their twenties,
choices.C: Her young students, many of whom are young and in their twenties,
choices.D: Her students, who are, many of them, young people in their twenties,

candidates.evidence: Her students, many of whom are young and in their twenties,
candidates.explanation: Being in one's twenties already means being young, so "young and" is redundant. B states the idea once.

A.rationale: "Young and in their twenties" repeats the same idea.

C.rationale: "Young" appears twice and repeats the idea again.

D.rationale: This is wordy and still repeats the idea.

hints: Does "in their twenties" already tell you they are young?
Choose the version without repetition.

strategy.explanation: All are grammatical; the concise one is best.

candidates.remember: Cut words that repeat an idea.

candidates.subskill: Evaluating whether an essay meets a stated goal
candidates.stem: Suppose the writer's goal had been to write an essay about the history of vinyl lettering technology. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.A: Yes, because it explains when vinyl lettering machines first appeared.
choices.B: Yes, because it describes why shop owners stopped using vinyl stickers.
choices.C: No, because it focuses on one sign painter's craft and career, mentioning vinyl lettering only as a challenge she faced.
choices.D: No, because it never mentions vinyl lettering or any other technology.

candidates.evidence: When vinyl lettering machines arrived in the 1990s, many of Marrow's customers switched.
candidates.explanation: The essay is about Edith Marrow: how she learned, the challenge vinyl posed, and her teaching today. Vinyl lettering appears in one paragraph as a challenge, not as the essay's subject.

A.rationale: The essay gives one date, but one fact does not make it a history of the technology.

B.rationale: This detail serves Marrow's story; the essay does not trace the technology's development.

D.rationale: The essay does mention vinyl lettering, in paragraph 3.

hints: What is the essay mainly about?
Is vinyl lettering the subject or one detail?

strategy.explanation: Decide yes or no from the main focus, then pick the accurate reason.

candidates.remember: Goal questions: compare the goal with the essay's main focus.
